known_information: The original report gives precise Ctrl+Left to Ctrl+PgUp and Ctrl+Up to PgUp mappings, with a stateful failure when alternating while Ctrl remains held.
The reporter answered the old version-confirmation request and the issue was reopened; a later participant confirms a related held-modifier failure.
The later Ctrl+LeftAlt workaround explicitly does not work with AltGr and is distinct from the original Ctrl-only case.
Current shortcut handling tracks common modifiers, invocation state and a special RightAlt/AltGr path; a historical4712fix does not prove every later state transition is repaired.
issue_context.summary: Investigate held-modifier restoration when alternating remapped action keys
initial_investigation: Read the entire detailed sequence, all reopen/version replies and the corrected AltGr workaround.
Read current-main common-modifier and AltGr restoration/reset paths. No current regression test execution or universal fix is claimed.
issue_context.analysis: Transitioning between a target that retains Ctrl and one that releases Ctrl may leave virtual/original modifier state inconsistent. Test the original Ctrl-only sequence separately from the later AltGr variant before changing common-modifier restoration.
inferences: The proposed mechanism is provisional and is not an executed runtime result or evidence that the old report is fixed.

prerequisites: Use a disposable test environment and test-owned documents/configuration; preserve existing user data.
reproduce.expected: Each configured action should remain responsive while its original modifier is held, and key-up should restore truthful state without requiring an unrelated remap to recover.
steps: Configure exactly Ctrl+Left to Ctrl+PgUp and Ctrl+Up to PgUp; in a test browser with disposable tabs hold Ctrl and alternate Left, Up, Left.
Release Ctrl, press it again, and repeat the documented recovery sequence while tracing original and virtual key state.
Compare left/right Ctrl and a separate Ctrl+LeftAlt versus AltGr mapping; create distinct regressions rather than merging their causes.
